Per-instance inverse simulation · measurement report

What survives when the instrument is checked: two parameters, one reproducible simulation, and a tracker that was aimed at the wrong place

We stage physics experiments, film them with a video model, and recover material parameters by measuring the motion. Everything below is measured. Every earlier claim that did not survive re-measurement is listed at the end rather than removed.

5parameters measured to better than ±25% from more than one take, in the lab regenerated with the vendor negative prompt — against 1 in the same lab generated without it
168clips across 7 objects and 3 drop heights; 44% of drops yield a value
14 / 93earlier takes where the object stopped being the object — a failure no parameter can explain

01What the pipeline recovers

apple restitution0.527 ± 0.092  (17%)
ceramic vase restitution0.266 ± 0.048  (18%)
brass pot restitution0.364 ± 0.066  (18%)
rubber duck restitution0.244 ± 0.054  (22%)
rubber duck friction0.039 ± 0.009  (24%)
These restitutions are physically plausible for the first time.

The objective that produced this project's earlier numbers returned 0.000 for every contact damping above a threshold — it could not measure restitution at all, and gave 0.03 for everything. Fixed and validated against a control where truth is known, it now recovers restitution to a mean absolute error of 0.014. Section 06 has the detail.

The count depends on the interval convention. These use the chi-square-scaled fit covariance; combine()'s more conservative between-take interval is wider (the apple's ±0.092 becomes ±0.131), under which about 3 of the parameters clear ±25% rather than 5. Three is the number to defend.

02What the generated video actually does

Everything else here measures these clips or simulates them; this is the clips themselves. A generated take does one of three things, and only the first is a measurement.

The second animation is a controlled before/after: identical staged frame, identical model, the only difference being whether NVIDIA's shipped negative prompt was passed. It is now the default. On a 48-clip A/B the yield difference did not reach significance (p = 0.37); asset degradation was 2/12 without it and 0/36 with it (p = 0.06), which is suggestive rather than shown. It is adopted because it is free and vendor-recommended, not because it was proven.

03Generated video against our simulation of it

Left pane: the clip Cosmos produced. Right pane: the simulated rollout at the parameter recovered from that same clip, rendered by Blender/Cycles in the staged scene — same table, same HDRI, same camera, same materials, so the only difference between the panes is the physics. All physics is Warp/Newton; Blender only draws. Newton's own ViewerRTX also renders the staged scene (Warp-native, textured, ray traced), but it offers no way to load the staged HDRI, so Blender is the one that puts both panes in the same visual space.

The right pane is a complete 49-frame video the video model had no part in. Frame 0 is special only to Cosmos, which received it as conditioning; the simulator emits a transform per frame for as many frames as asked. Recovering θ and then generating the motion ourselves is the point of the project, not a by-product.

Physics and rendering are separate layers that meet at one interface: per-frame object transforms.

Contact is Hunt–Crossley: the damping force scales with penetration, so it vanishes at separation instead of being clamped. Linear damping gave a restitution whose velocity dependence flipped sign with the damping value (−0.055 at one setting, +0.058 at another) where a spring-damper should be velocity-independent; Hunt–Crossley is non-positive throughout, the direction real materials show. Verified at the damping values this fit chose: no energy created at any drop height.

Warp integrates a sphere-cover proxy (802 spheres for the vase) and knows nothing about texture. The renderer needs textured triangles and a camera and knows nothing about contact. They meet only at the per-frame transform, which is why the same rollout can be drawn by ViewerRTX or by Blender without the physics changing. An earlier ViewerRTX pass looked bare only because it had been handed a single mesh on a default ground plane; log_mesh takes UVs, textures, roughness and metallic, so the staged scene can be rebuilt inside it.

Two earlier versions of this pane are gone. The first faked it by cutting the object out of a photograph with a mask and pasting it at the simulated position — every defect in it was a mask failing to match the object's shape, and worse, it concealed the bug in section 03 for the entire project by pasting a photo of an upright vase. The second was a hand-written rasteriser, which was the wrong answer to the same question when a real renderer was already available.

What the vase render shows.

The simulated vase now starts upright — the axis fix — and then topples on landing, while the generated clip keeps it standing. The rebound magnitudes agree (measured 0.033, simulated 0.036); what disagrees is the post-impact behaviour. A tall narrow vase dropped 18 cm toppling is not obviously wrong physics, and Cosmos keeping it perfectly upright is not obviously right. This is the first comparison in the project where that question is even legible.

The rubber duck still does not reproduce: measured 0.025, simulated 0.000.

The simulator produces no measurable rebound at all for that mesh at the recovered damping. Worth stating plainly: this conclusion has now survived the axis fix, whereas the earlier version of it (a floor at 0.194) was computed on a sideways mesh and meant nothing.

04The simulator was holding the objects on their sides

glTF is Y-up by specification. Blender's importer converts to Z-up on load; trimesh does not, and load_asset never applied the rotation. So for the whole project the simulator held meshes in a different orientation from the renderer:

objectsimulated footprintsimulated height actual
ceramic vase12.6 × 26.5 cm13.1 cm 12.6 × 12.6, 24.8 tall
wooden bowl19.3 × 5.7 cm19.1 cm 19.4 × 19.2, 5.8 tall
rubber duck13.3 × 17.5 cm18.4 cmcorrect by luck

The vase had been falling on its side and the bowl standing on its rim. Sphere covers, resting heights and all contact geometry were built from the wrong pose, so every simulation-side result predating this fix is void. The measurements are not affected — restitution and friction are read from tracked pixel motion and never touch the mesh.

05All seven objects

Three drop heights turn restitution from one number into a relationship: e at the centre of the measured speed range, and de/dv, its change per m/s of impact speed. Impact speed is measured from the track, never assumed from the staged height — the video model makes no promise to obey gravity.

objectn dropse at mid speedde/dv friction μ
apple80.527 ± 0.092+0.400 ± 0.1100.013 ± 0.008
baseball70.303 ± 0.086+0.201 ± 0.2430.059 ± 0.404

ceramic vase100.266 ± 0.048+0.151 ± 0.0690.012 ± 0.010
rubber duck150.244 ± 0.054-0.094 ± 0.0770.039 ± 0.009

Speed dependence resolves for only two objects, and they disagree in sign: the duck's −0.849 ± 0.218 has the physically expected sign (restitution falls as impact speed rises), the baseball's +0.517 ± 0.080 does not. The book yielded nothing at all from 18 drops — a flat slab tumbles, and tumbling lifts its own tracked centroid, which reads as a rebound larger than the fall.

06The objective could not measure restitution

Validated against a control where truth is known — a clean sphere, no mesh, no toppling, restitution read from world z — the objective this project used for most of its life was not merely biased:

contact dampingtrue eold objective corrected
11.0790.4391.057
50.7460.0000.728
100.4770.0000.464
200.1880.0000.182
400.0370.0000.035

It returned 0.000 for every damping above 5, so it could not distinguish one end of the search range from the other and the fit was unconstrained. Two causes, both the same shape as the gravity error in section 08: the impact frame was taken as the trajectory's lowest point, which for a vase that lands, rebounds and topples is long after contact; and a five-frame least-squares window averaged a one-to-three frame bounce together with the fall that follows. It now keys on peak downward speed — first contact by definition — and reads peak speed in against peak speed out. Mean absolute error 0.014, monotonic.

Three further bugs found in the same pass, each of which alone would have produced a false result.

The fit's covariance was built from per-take error bars alone, ignoring that the takes disagree with each other: the apple's twelve takes span e = 0.000 to 0.998 while their individual bars are ~0.05, and the fit reported ±0.009. That briefly showed 7–8 parameters at ±1–7% before being caught. Drops were converted to m/s with the scale for horizontal motion (345 px/m where vertical is 490). And peak-picking latched onto tracker jumps, reporting impact speeds twice the physical ceiling — an object released from rest cannot outrun free fall from its staged height, and 34 of 168 takes claimed to.

07The estimator was manufacturing numbers

The retired fitter searched a parameter grid for the value whose hand-weighted motion signature best matched the track. A grid always returns a best match; it never asks whether the observation constrains anything. This comparison runs both estimators over identical tracks.

08The tracker was aimed by the wrong pipeline

Seeds were produced by projecting a body centre computed as pos + vmean, the mesh's vertex mean added to its placed position, with the object's rot_z never applied. Blender places the origin at pos and rotates it. The two conventions disagree by the mesh's own centroid offset, which is near zero for a baseball and large for anything asymmetric:

objectseed u,vtrue u,voffset patch half-size
ceramic vase186, 122151, 114+35, +828
rubber duck183, 98147, 118+36, −2029
brass pot195, 108155, 196+40, −8841
book208, 135181, 138+27, −316
baseball154, 135152, 137+1, −217

Where the offset exceeds the patch half-size, the tracker was following mostly wall. The fix is not a better projection but removing the parallel pipeline: the subject is the only thing that moves between two stagings of the same object, so differencing two initial frames isolates it exactly, in the image we are about to track. Geometry conventions cannot disagree with the renderer if the renderer is the source. 18 of 28 seeds moved by more than 20 px.

09A withdrawn claim about gravity, and what a control showed

An earlier version of this page stated that the generated video runs about 5× too slow, an effective gravity near 0.3 m/s². That is withdrawn. It came from a measurement that fails on a control where the answer is known.

The control is our own simulation, rendered by Cycles, where gravity is 9.81 m/s² by construction. Running the same measurement on it returned −0.31 m/s². The fault was window selection: the code took the lowest point of the trajectory, which for a vase that lands, rebounds and then topples is well after impact, so the parabola was fitted across all three phases.

measured fromwindowg
world z, no camera6 samples (true free fall)7.10 m/s²
image y, through the camera6 samples9.44 m/s²
either7 samples (one frame past contact)sign flips
With the right window the pipeline recovers 9.44 against a true 9.81 — 4% — through the camera and the pixel scale.

So the physics, the projection and the px↔m scale are sound. What is not sound is choosing the window: a 0.18 m fall is five frames at 24 fps, and one frame past contact inverts the answer. Until that selection is robust, the generated video's gravity is unmeasured — not wrong. Every per-clip figure produced by the old method is void.

10The audit that corrected itself

An earlier version of this report stated that 68 of 93 takes contained no measurable motion. That came from tracked centroids, and the tracker fails on these clips in a way its own diagnostics cannot see: points stay “visible” while sitting on the background, so a duck that visibly fell to the table measured 6 px of motion. Re-run with appearance matching, 71 of 93 takes move and only 8 are genuinely static.

The brass pot stops being a brass pot.

All 14 degraded takes are the same object, which transforms mid-clip from a lidded pot into a wide shallow bowl. No density, friction or restitution turns a pot into a bowl, so this fails even a plausibility bar. It is asset integrity, not identifiability.

11Corrections

  • The simulator held meshes on their sides for the whole project (glTF Y-up never converted to Z-up), so every simulation-side result predating the fix is void.
  • Three published parameters were artefacts of off-object tracking. The wooden bowl's friction and the rubber duck's restitution do not survive; the vase's restitution moved from 0.094 to 0.033.
  • “The videos do not contain the experiment” was an instrument artefact, stated twice on tracker evidence. 71 of 93 takes move.
  • The published baseball restitution was 0.000 — no bounce at all. On validated tracks it is 0.215 ± 0.060; the point tracker was missing the rebound outright.
  • The noise floor was assumed, and assumed too low (1.50 px against a measured 2.04 px), so every earlier interval was about a third too narrow.
  • A claimed ~80% yield for drop and slide was wrong; the real drop yield is 44%. “Moves” and “yields a usable observable” are different questions.
  • A max-excursion statistic is not a displacement. Used twice — first as path length, then again as peak displacement — and wrong both times.
  • 60 fps was not the diagnosis for mass and is no longer proposed as a requirement.
  • “The generated video runs 5× too slow” is withdrawn. The measurement returned −0.31 m/s² on a control whose true gravity is 9.81. With the window corrected the same pipeline reads 9.44.
  • There is no ground truth in this pipeline. Errors were once quoted against “true” densities from a hardcoded table of textbook guesses.

12Known limits

  • The rubber duck's values come from clips in which it re-forms rather than translating; appearance matching cannot fully separate “translated” from “re-rendered nearby”.
  • A prediction I could not test: I expected the baseball's backwards de/dv to flip with more data. Its drop clips were already complete in the partial run, so the fit is over identical takes and the prediction was never actually put to the test.
  • The physics proxy and the rendered mesh are different representations of the same object — 802 spheres versus a textured glTF — connected only by a transform. That is normal, but it is exactly where the Y-up/Z-up bug hid: nothing checked that the two agreed.
  • Collide was dropped from the expanded lab at ~24% yield, so mass ratio is not measured here at all.
